import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Green's Open Problem 44

*References:*
- [Gr24] [Ben Green's 100 Open Problems](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.44)
- [Er80] Erdős, Paul. "A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory."
  Annals of Discrete Mathematics 6 (1980): 89-115.
-/

namespace Green44

open scoped Nat

/--
Sieve $[N]$ by removing half the residue classes mod $p_i$, for primes
$2 \leqslant p_1 < p_2 < \dots < p_{1000} < N^{9/10}$. Does the remaining set have size at most
$\frac{1}{10} N$?

We interpret "half the residue classes" as $\lfloor p_i / 2 \rfloor$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem green_44 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (N : ℕ) (p : Fin 1000 → ℕ) (A : (i : Fin 1000) → Finset (ZMod (p i))),
      let remaining := (Finset.Icc 1 N).filter (fun x => ∀ i, (x : ZMod (p i)) ∉ A i)
      (∀ i, (p i).Prime) →
      StrictMono p →
      (p 999) ^ 10 < N ^ 9 →
      (∀ i, (A i).card = (p i) / 2) →
      10 * remaining.card ≤ N := by
  sorry

/-- The answer is affirmative if the primes are all less than $N^{1/2}$, by the large sieve. [Gr24] -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem green_44.variants.less_than_sqrt :
    ∀ (N : ℕ) (p : Fin 1000 → ℕ) (A : (i : Fin 1000) → Finset (ZMod (p i))),
      let remaining := (Finset.Icc 1 N).filter (fun x => ∀ i, (x : ZMod (p i)) ∉ A i)
      (∀ i, (p i).Prime) →
      StrictMono p →
      (p 999) ^ 2 < N →
      (∀ i, (A i).card = (p i) / 2) →
      10 * remaining.card ≤ N := by
  sorry

end Green44

findings.description: The unrestricted `∀ (N : ℕ)` makes the right-hand side elementarily false, suggesting a missing sufficiently-large-N convention. Take N = 100000 and enumerate the 1000 primes in [20011, 30161]. For each prime q, remove the residue classes represented by (q+1)/2 ≤ r < q. These are exactly floor(q/2) classes, and none meets {1,…,10001}. All hypotheses hold, including 30161^10 < 100000^9, but 10 * remaining.card ≥ 100010 > 100000. The negation of the exact Lean right-hand side was proved in /workspace/review/counterexample.lean; native_decide certifies the finite prime count. The counterexample is certain, but the classification is qualified because Green's wording does not explicitly specify that N is sufficiently large: clarification is needed to distinguish an omitted asymptotic convention from a problem with the source's literal formulation.
findings.source_evidence: Green, 100 Open Problems, Problem 44, pp. 22–23 (https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.44), asks whether removing half the classes for 1000 primes below N^(9/10) leaves at most N/10 integers, and presents this as an open sieve question. Its comments cite Erdős, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory, §6, Problem 3, p. 107 (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1980-03.pdf). Erdős asks a more general question with an existential number k = k₀(ε,η) of primes and calls the general case intractable. Neither passage explicitly resolves the N-quantifier for Green's fixed-1000 formulation; the natural nontrivial reading must avoid the finite counterexample above.
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify the intended N-range. For the asymptotic reading, replace `∀ (N : ℕ) (p : ...) (A : ...), ...` with `∀ᶠ (N : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∀ (p : ...) (A : ...), ...`, retaining the other conditions. The eventual quantifier must precede both p and A so that the threshold is uniform over the sieve choices. Document 'for all sufficiently large N'.

reformulations.difference: Lean bounds only the last indexed prime using `(p 999)^2 < N`, and writes the conclusion as `10 * remaining.card ≤ N`, rather than bounding every prime by √N and the remaining cardinality by N/10.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Fin 1000 has last index 999, and StrictMono makes p 999 the largest prime. For nonnegative natural p and N, p² < N is equivalent to (p : ℝ) < √N. Multiplying the real cardinality bound by the positive number 10 gives exactly the natural-number inequality. The full equivalence of these two versions of the square-root statement was proved in /workspace/review/equivalences.lean without using either problem theorem.

sources_consulted: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf — January 2026 version; notation on p. 2 and Problem 44 with comments on pp. 22–23
https://arxiv.org/e-print/1311.6176 — Green–Harper, Inverse questions for the large sieve; LaTeX source, §2 classical large sieve proposition
could_not_verify: Green44.green_44: the literal all-N proposition is conclusively refuted, but the source leaves its intended N-quantification implicit. Whether the formalization omits a large-N convention or faithfully reproduces an overly literal source formulation requires clarification.
review.notes: Both declarations and their definitions were checked. The prime hypotheses exclude ZMod 0 and ZMod 1; the interval and filtering encode the intended sieve. Natural division gives the documented floor, agreeing with Erdős's (p−1)/2 for odd primes. The main integer-power condition was also proved equivalent to the real N^(9/10) condition. The square-root variant has no finite-size defect: the classical large sieve gives |R| ≤ (N+Q²)/(Σ floor(p_i/2)/p_i) < 6N/1000 < N/10, since Q²<N and each summand is at least 1/3. The current Green source still presents the main problem as open and the square-root case as affirmative; no source-recorded status discrepancy was found. The reviewed file was not modified.
